newsitem.title: USA: Greenspan policy reflects job mandate commitment.
newsitem.headline: Greenspan policy reflects job mandate commitment.

text.p: The Federal Reserve under chairman Alan Greenspan has never hiked the federal funds rate after an increase in the unemployment rate, underscoring the U.S. central bank's commitment to its job growth mandate, a Fed source told Reuters.

"We all are influenced by NAIRU (non-accelerating inflation rate of unemployment) to a certain extent," a senior Fed official said, answering a question about the relationship between the jobless rate and Fed policy. "But the Fed is by no means anti-job creation."
"But the Fed is by no means anti-job creation," the source added, noting a declining inflation trend allowed the Fed to cut rates in 1995 even though the jobless rate was low.
The Fed's dual Congressional mandate calls for the central bank to seek low inflation as well as maximum employment.
The source also noted the Fed never cited the jobless rate as a reason for tightening credit during its 1994 cycle.

Nomura Securities International chief economist David Resler noted, "We can find no instance in which the Fed, under Greenspan, raised interest rates when the unemployment rate had increased in its most recent report."
Since becoming chairman in August 1987, Greenspan almost never raised rates when the latest unemployment rate available showed an increase -- regardless of the jobless rate level.

The one exception was in June 1988, when the Fed raised the funds rate by 25 basis points as the unemployment rate edged up by 0.2 percentage point to 5.6 percent -- still below its level before the 1987 stock market crash.
"This shows the Fed, besides its primary emphasis on inflation, remains sensitive to its dual mandate," Resler also said. "The Fed is pursuing its dual objective by making sure inflation stays low."
Resler pointed out the absence of Fed tightening despite a historically low unemployment level has made the case that robust job creation is not a factor in Fed policy.
"This shows inflation, and not healthy job creation, is the factor that triggers Fed tightenings," Resler, a former St. Louis Fed economist, added.
Resler noted the main feature of Fed policy under Greenspan has been its preemptive nature.
"1996 may be called the year of preemptive inaction," Resler said of the Fed's absence of a move based on the central bank's forecast for slower growth.
"People think about policy as changes in policy. But we have three examples of Fed policy implying a forward-looking approach," Resler also said.
"In 1994, we had preemtpive tightening, in 1995, preemptive easing and in 1996, preemptive inaction, because the Fed believed the acceleration of growth would be short-lived," Resler added.
Wrightson Associates chief economist Lou Crandall said Greenspan does not focus on abstract notions -- such as the unemployment rate.

"The notion there might be some fixed level of unemployment that is the unique inflation threshold is hard to accept," Crandall said. "The unemployment does not affect Greenspan's views very much. The way he looks at it is to see how sternly he should evaluate other evidence. He still looks for confirmation from more direct inflation gauges."
